claims.text: Conventional powder consolidation of W particles or connected W regions in a Cu matrix exhibits phase separation, voids, and poor interfacial contact.
W particles will be pre-coated with a thin, uniform Cu film by vapor deposition before consolidation.
Vapor-deposited Cu pre-coating will produce a more uniform W–Cu composite.
Vapor-deposited Cu pre-coating will produce a defect-free W–Cu composite.
Vapor-deposited Cu pre-coating will improve thermal transport in W–Cu.
Vapor-deposited Cu pre-coating will maintain mechanical durability under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints.
A preformed conformal Cu layer will enhance interfacial bonding between Cu and W.
A conformal Cu layer will promote near-perfect W/Cu contact.
A conformal Cu layer will minimize voids at particle boundaries.
The Cu coating will minimize phase separation by establishing immediate and continuous metallic contact during sintering.
Continuous W/Cu metallic contact during sintering will reduce void and defect formation.
Improved W/Cu interfaces will provide efficient thermal bridging between W and Cu.
The improved W/Cu interface will resist irradiation-induced interfacial degradation.
Relative to spark-plasma sintering of uncoated W particles, the coated composite will have lower porosity and greater W/Cu interfacial uniformity.
Lower porosity and greater interfacial uniformity will yield superior thermal transport.
The coated composite will maintain or improve mechanical durability relative to the uncoated baseline after irradiation.
Induction melting, arc-plasma casting, and standard powder metallurgy often produce phase separation, voids, and nonuniform W/Cu interfaces.
Rapid sintering will retain a fine W–Cu microstructure.
Processing below the W melting point and Cu boiling point will preserve the coated interface during consolidation.
The relevant service regime is high-temperature irradiation typical of fusion-reactor joints.
